source_read: PMC HTML full text PMC8324483 (Lancet Oncol 22(8):1071-1080), read in full in my own browser tab: Summary, Research in context panel, Introduction, Methods, Results with the Table (HTML), Discussion, funding, interests and acknowledgments. Figure 4 (cases by 10 g/day band and sex) viewed on its PMC figure page; Figures 1-3 (regional PAFs and maps) not needed for these claims. The supplementary appendix (mmc1, which holds the relative-risk functions, consumption methods and regional tables) not read.

claims.overstatement: Framed as a model estimate throughout, with the right counterfactual (lifetime abstention), and no advice. Small wording points. (1) 'Drinking estimated from 2010 sales and surveys': the paper's sources are recorded, unrecorded and tourist per-capita consumption (GISAH), with survey data used for the distribution of drinking. 'Sales' covers only the recorded part; 'per-capita consumption data and surveys' would be exact. (2) 'Liver (hepatocellular carcinoma only) 154,700, 17.3%': as with the oesophagus, the 17.3% is of all liver cancers, not of hepatocellular carcinoma (Table footnote); the claim says so for the oesophagus but not for the liver. (3) 'The model counts only the cancers ...' would read better as 'includes only', given the next sentence. (4) The paper's drink is implicitly 10 g ('<20 g, up to two drinks'), unlike Bagnardi's 12.5 g; the claim's 'up to about two drinks' follows the paper. Omitted qualifier: the totals are gross, not net. The model does not subtract kidney cancers that WCRF judges probably reduced by up to 30 g/day (Methods, 1st paragraph). Comparison group: 'lifetime abstention' is the model's counterfactual, and the claim names it correctly. The main text does not say which reference group the WCRF relative risks themselves used (lifetime abstainers, all non-drinkers, or the lowest intake; appendix not read), so the claim should not imply the risk estimates were measured against lifetime abstainers.
claims.note: All numbers from this source match the Summary, Results and Table. 741,300 (558,500-951,200), 4.1% (3.1-5.3); men 568,700 (422,500-731,100), 6.1% (4.6-7.9); women 172,600 (135,900-220,100), 2.0% (1.6-2.5). All eight site figures with intervals and fractions match. By intake: 346,400 (46.7%), 291,800 (39.4%), 103,100 (13.9%; 82,600-207,200), and under 10 g/day 41,300 (35,400-145,800), with men 16,700 (14,300-75,400) and women 24,600 (21,100-70,400). Sensitivity totals 808,700 (616,300-1,034,800; 4.5%) and 925,900 (705,900-1,187,500; 5.2%) match, as do earlier estimates of 5.5% (cases, 2012), 4.8% (deaths, 2016) and 4.9% (deaths, 2019). Funding: none; no competing interests. Editors' arithmetic, recomputed: the site figures sum to 741,200 (741,300 with rounding); the men's site figures sum to 568,700 and the women's to 172,600; the intake bands sum to 741,300; 346.4/741.3 = 46.7%, 291.8/741.3 = 39.4%, 103.1/741.3 = 13.9%; 24,600/172,600 = 14.3% and 16,700/568,700 = 2.9%; 741,300 + 50,000 (pancreas) + 17,400 (stomach) = 808,700. 925,900 - 741,300 = 184,600, not the stated 135,000 (nor does 135,000 fit 925,900 - 808,700 = 117,200); men 713,200 + women 212,700 = 925,900, so the totals agree with each other and the stated increment is the odd figure: I get the same as the claim. 'About 4, 6 and 2 in 100' match 4.1%, 6.1% and 2.0%. Model description confirmed: IARC sufficient-evidence sites; HCC and SCC subtype estimates, with HCC from unpublished work (Rumgay H); WCRF CUP relative risks for current drinking, from meta-analyses of cohort studies; 2010 consumption with a 10-year latency; former drinking only in sensitivity analysis; no population-specific RRs; UIs from 1000 simulated draws of drinking status, mean and SD of consumption, and RRs only. That the UIs leave out incidence, latency and model structure is the editors' inference from that list, and a fair one. The low-intake intervals are lopsided (Figure 4). Not from this source: Rehm et al. 2009 (487 thousand deaths) and Griswold et al. 2018 (27.1%, 18.9%). Rumgay does not cite Rehm 2009, but Rehm and Shield are co-authors here, which supports 'overlapping team'.

anchors.locator: Summary › Findings; Results, 1st paragraph; Table, 'All sites excluding non-melanoma skin cancer' row
anchors.extracted: Estimated 741,300 (95% UI 558,500-951,200) new cancer cases in 2020 attributable to alcohol, PAF 4.1% (3.1-5.3). Males 568,700 (422,500-731,100; 76.7% of attributable cases), PAF 6.1% (4.6-7.9); females 172,600 (135,900-220,100; 23.3%), PAF 2.0% (1.6-2.5). Age-standardised rate 8.4 (6.2-10.9) per 100,000 (males 13.4, females 3.7). All sites exclude non-melanoma skin cancer (C44).

anchors.locator: Table (by cancer site, both sexes) and its footnotes
anchors.extracted: Attributable cases (95% UI), PAF: lip and oral cavity 74,900 (44,600-119,600), 20.2%; pharynx 39,400 (16,100-67,800), 22.0%; oesophagus 189,700 (110,900-274,600), 31.6%; colon 91,500 (68,300-114,500), 8.1%; rectum 65,100 (48,500-82,000), 9.0%; liver 154,700 (43,700-281,500), 17.3%; larynx 27,600 (15,700-43,300), 15.0%; female breast 98,300 (68,200-130,500), 4.4%. Footnotes: oesophageal cases computed as squamous cell carcinoma and liver cases as hepatocellular carcinoma; the PAFs are of all oesophageal and all liver cancers. Oesophageal PAF 39.2% in males vs 14.3% in females (Results, 1st paragraph).

anchors.locator: Methods › Study design and data sources, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Sites selected from the latest IARC monograph (vol 100E) as those with sufficient evidence of a causal link; incidence from GLOBOCAN 2020. HCC and oesophageal SCC distributions were taken from two studies, with the HCC estimates unpublished (Rumgay H). Stomach and pancreas, which WCRF but not IARC classes as causal, appear only in sensitivity analysis. A possible reduction in kidney cancer (WCRF: probable protective evidence up to 30 g/day) was deliberately not included.

anchors.locator: Methods › Study design and data sources, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Relative risks for current drinking came from WCRF Continuous Update Project reviews. Former drinking (lifetime use but none in the past 12 months) appears only in sensitivity analysis. A 10-year latency was assumed, so 2010 adult per-capita consumption from GISAH (by age group and sex) was used and converted to g/day. Per-capita data combine recorded, unrecorded and tourist consumption.

Levin-based PAF, adapted from Shield et al., against a theoretical minimum-risk exposure of lifetime abstention. PAFs combine the prevalence of current drinking with RRs of current drinking, integrated up to 150 g/day. Categories: moderate under 20 g/day ('up to two drinks'), risky 20-60 g, heavy over 60 g ('more than six'), which implies about 10 g per drink; also 10 g/day bands. UIs from a Monte Carlo-like simulation of 1000 draws of drinking status, mean and SD of consumption, and RRs (2.5th-97.5th percentiles). Incidence, latency and model choices were not simulated.

By intake: under 20 g/day 103,100 (13.9%; 82,600-207,200); 20-60 g 291,800 (39.4%; 227,700-333,100); over 60 g 346,400 (46.7%; 227,900-489,400). Under 10 g/day: 41,300 (35,400-145,800), of which males 16,700 (14,300-75,400; 2.9% of male attributable cases) and females 24,600 (21,100-70,400; 14.3% of female cases). The most cases were in males at 30-50 g/day and females at 10-30 g/day. Figure 4: the 0-10 g bars have upper error bars far above the point estimates (about 75,000 for males, 70,000 for females).

Adding stomach and pancreas: total 808,700 (616,300-1,034,800), PAF 4.5% (3.4-5.8), comprising pancreas 50,000 (13,200-95,900; PAF 10.1%) and stomach 17,400 (810-36,900; PAF 1.6%). Including former drinking 'added' 135,000 (102,200-171,900) cases for a total of 925,900 (705,900-1,187,500; males 713,200, females 212,700), PAF 5.2% (3.9-6.6). Editors' arithmetic: 925,900 - 741,300 = 184,600, not 135,000.

Earlier global estimates were 5.5% of cancer cases in 2012 (Praud), 4.8% of cancer deaths in 2016 (Shield) and 4.9% of cancer deaths in 2019 (GBD 2019). The paper gives these reasons for the differences: falls in consumption; HCC rather than all liver cancer (HCC is about 80% of primary liver cancer, unpublished); Praud including pancreas and gallbladder (about 40,000 cases); Shield including former drinking; and earlier studies estimating deaths rather than cases.

The authors call the estimates conservative: only IARC sites and only current drinking. Stated strengths: RRs from meta-analyses of high-quality cohort studies, and a prevalence model that corrects survey under-reporting with per-capita data. Stated limitations: no adjustment for differential under-reporting by age and sex or for changes in consumption before or after 2010; survey bias under-estimating former drinkers; and uneven data quality between countries, especially where unrecorded consumption is high or national surveys are lacking.

No alcohol-tobacco interaction was modelled. Some attributed cases could be due to tobacco through residual confounding in the RRs, and some liver cases to hepatitis B or C or aflatoxin. Obesity was not considered. The same RRs were used in every population (possible under-estimate in eastern Asian ALDH2*2 carriers), and prospective studies from low- and middle-income settings are scarce. The 2020 incidence estimates do not reflect COVID-19 disruptions to diagnosis.
PAFs for ten countries without alcohol prevalence data were imputed from regional averages.

anchors.locator: Summary › Funding; Methods › Role of the funding source; Declaration of interests; Acknowledgments; author list
anchors.extracted: No funding source; the authors declare no competing interests. The first author's work was done during a PhD studentship at IARC, and some authors are IARC/WHO staff. The authors include K Shield and J Rehm, authors of the earlier models.

claims.overstatement: The Rumgay figure is correctly presented as a model attribution against lifetime abstention. Two qualifiers could be added: the low-intake figure is gross, not net (kidney cancers that WCRF judges probably reduced up to 30 g/day are not subtracted), and former drinkers count as unexposed in the main analysis. The point that it depends on the low-intake shape of the risk curves is fair: the curves are WCRF's and appear only in the appendix (not read).
claims.note: 41,300 (35,400-145,800) for under 10 g/day matches Results, 4th paragraph, and the 'against lifetime abstention' counterfactual matches Methods › Statistical analysis, 1st paragraph. The interval is strongly lopsided (upper bound 3.5 times the estimate); Figure 4 shows the same for each sex. 'Up to 10 g' is the paper's under-10 g/day band. The Bagnardi and Griswold parts of the claim are not from this source.

anchors.extracted: Under 10 g/day: 41,300 (95% UI 35,400-145,800) attributable cases in 2020 (males 16,700, 14,300-75,400; females 24,600, 21,100-70,400). Under 20 g/day: 103,100 (82,600-207,200), 13.9% of the total. Figure 4 shows the 0-10 g bars with upper error bars far above the estimates.

anchors.locator: Methods › Statistical analysis, 1st and 4th paragraphs; Methods › Study design and data sources, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Counterfactual is lifetime abstention. RRs are for current drinking (WCRF CUP), applied identically to all countries; former drinking appears only in sensitivity analysis. UIs reflect only simulated drinking and RR uncertainty. Only IARC sites are counted, and the probable protective association for kidney cancer up to 30 g/day is deliberately not subtracted.

claims.note: Rumgay used the IARC monograph (vol 100E) list of sites with sufficient evidence of causation: lip and oral cavity, pharynx, oesophagus (SCC), colon, rectum, liver (HCC), larynx and female breast. These match the sites the claim names as associated with drinking above 12.5 g/day. Further qualifiers relevant to this claim: stomach and pancreas are causal for WCRF but not for IARC (sensitivity analysis only), and WCRF rates the evidence for a protective association with kidney cancer up to 30 g/day as probable. That bears on the claim's kidney finding.

anchors.locator: Methods › Study design and data sources, 1st paragraph; Introduction, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Cancer types selected from the latest IARC monograph (vol 100E) with sufficient evidence of a causal relationship: oral cavity, pharynx, larynx, oesophagus (SCC), colon, rectum, liver (HCC) and female breast. Together these accounted for 6.3 million cases and 3.3 million deaths in 2020 (GLOBOCAN). Stomach and pancreas are causal under WCRF but lack sufficient IARC evidence, so appear only in sensitivity analysis. WCRF rates the evidence that alcohol up to 30 g/day protects against kidney cancer as probable; this was not modelled.

key_findings.correction: Figure 4 viewed on its PMC figure page: the 0-10 g/day bars (about 16,700 for men, 24,600 for women) have upper error bars near 75,000 and 70,000, consistent with the text. Peaks are at 30-50 g/day for men and 10-30 g/day for women, as stated.

Recomputed: 2100/2800 = 75.0%, 34,800/49,900 = 69.7%, 590/1400 = 42.1%, 990/2700 = 36.7%, against printed 72.9%, 69.7%, 43.4% and 37.2%. Same reading as the card's note: the printed counts are rounded.
The 0.1-150 g/day limits were checked on the rendered formula (MathJax, Statistical analysis, 1st paragraph). The text itself states only the upper limit.

reporting_issues.note: Recomputed: 184,600 overall, +144,500 men and +40,100 women. 741,300 + 135,000 = 876,300 and 808,700 + 135,000 = 943,700; neither is 925,900. PAF 5.2% and the rate of 10.3 fit 925,900 better (ratios 1.25 and 1.23 against 1.18 for 876,300).

Recomputed: male cases per unit of rate are about 41,000-44,000 at other sites against about 20,600 for pharynx. The male interval (0.7-3.1) scales by the same factor as its point estimate, so this looks like a systematic error in the male pharyngeal rates rather than a single misprint. Both sexes: 39,400/0.5 = about 79,000 per unit, near the other rows (83,000-93,000). But the interval 0.4-1.6 does not fit the case interval (16,100-67,800 would give about 0.2-0.9).

risk_of_bias.note: Some concerns overall for the headline total, which comes mostly (86%) from intake of 20 g/day or more. For the low-intake outputs (below 20 and below 10 g/day) on their own, I would rate the relative-risk-curve domain high, not some concerns. Those figures rest entirely on the unshown low-intake shape of the WCRF curves, and their upper bounds reach 2 to 3.5 times the point estimates. Claims using those figures should carry that.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor. Causation is a model input taken from IARC, and the 'conservative' argument is one-sided, as the card says.

missed: Every both-sexes uncertainty bound in the Table equals the sum of the men's and women's bounds, within rounding. Examples: all sites 422,500 + 135,900 = about 558,500 and 731,100 + 220,100 = 951,200; under 10 g/day 14,300 + 21,100 = 35,400 and 75,400 + 70,400 = 145,800; oesophagus 94,200 + 16,700 = 110,900. So the sex-specific draws were treated as perfectly correlated (or the bounds were added), and the total intervals are the widest the sex-specific ones allow. This is minor, but it bears on how the intervals are read.
